The hedge fund that blew up in four days, and most of the world never saw it coming

In March 2021, Bill Hwang's family office, Archegos Capital, was one of the largest investors in a handful of US and Chinese stocks, including ViacomCBS, Discovery, Baidu, and Tencent Music. Yet almost nobody could tell. Hwang had roughly $10 billion of his own capital, and through borrowed money he controlled positions estimated at $50 billion or more, with some estimates higher. On paper, he looked like a modest holder. In reality, he was one of the biggest players in those names.

The trick was a financial product called a total return swap. Instead of buying shares directly, Archegos entered contracts with banks like Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, and Credit Suisse. The bank bought the shares and held them, Archegos got the profits and losses, and in exchange Archegos paid a fee and posted collateral. The shares showed up in the bank's name, not his, so the public filings that normally reveal big holders didn't show the full picture. Several banks competed for his business, and each one saw only its own slice, with no one seeing the total.

On March 22 and 23, ViacomCBS announced a stock sale and the shares dropped sharply. The collateral backing Archegos's positions shrank, and the banks issued margin calls, demanding more cash. Archegos couldn't pay. By March 26, the banks began dumping blocks of stock on the open market, ViacomCBS fell by more than half in days, and the forced selling spread through the rest of his portfolio. Credit Suisse lost about $5.5 billion and Nomura over $2 billion. Hwang was later convicted of fraud and racketeering and sentenced to 18 years in prison.

Here's the technical detail retail traders should take from it. Leverage doesn't just magnify a loss. It sets a price at which someone else decides to sell for you. When a position is financed with borrowed money, there is a level where the lender demands more collateral, and if you can't supply it, they sell at whatever the market will pay. In a fast move, that sale doesn't happen at the price where the call was issued. It happens lower, and the selling itself pushes the price down further, which triggers more calls. That chain reaction is what turned a bad week into a total loss.

The second lesson is concentration. His portfolio had a few big, correlated bets, which means that when one fell, the rest were hit too. A diversified-looking list of tickers can hide that kind of shared risk.

For a retail account, the same mechanics apply at smaller scale in any margin account, leveraged ETF, or heavily sized options position. The transferable habit is to know your liquidation level before you open the trade. Find where your broker would start forcing sales, ask what a 15% gap against you would do to that number, and size so you have room. If a position only survives when nothing goes wrong, it's too big, no matter how good the idea looks.

Trump administration officials went to Oracle with concerns about its chip leasing contract with Tencent, and the deal has since been cancelled, two people familiar with the matter told the Financial Times.

The five-year lease, worth an estimated $7 billion, would have given the Chinese tech giant access to as many as 100,000 advanced AI chips across a string of Oracle data centers in Southeast Asia, chips it can't use at home because of curbs from both Washington and Beijing. It was Tencent's largest overseas leasing deal. Top officials in Guangdong, where Tencent is based, also visited the company and asked it to back domestic Chinese chips, according to one of the people.

Overseas leasing deals like this one are allowed under existing rules, as the FT notes, so no regulation forced Oracle's hand. The contract was cancelled after officials raised their concerns with a company led by billionaire Trump backer Larry Ellison.

The cancellation landed a day after the FT reported that Nvidia has told data center and cloud customers that at least 51% of their services must go to non-Chinese companies, a requirement five people said it had never imposed before and has delivered verbally. That rule covers only new contracts and leaves existing agreements alone. Tencent's lease was signed earlier this year, so Oracle walked away from a contract Nvidia's own rule would have left in place.

In a statement to AFP, Nvidia said: "America cannot win the AI race unless America's AI infrastructure wins worldwide." Meanwhile, Chinese foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said she was not aware of the report. One Singapore-based cloud group told FT it is hard to find enough non-Chinese customers outside the US.

Washington has spent most of the year trying to close the remote access loophole: US export controls cover where a chip is shipped, not who rents time on it abroad. The Remote Access Security Act, which would put remote access under export-control law, passed the House 369-22 in January and then stalled in the Senate Banking Committee. Commerce has been drafting its own rule to block Chinese firms from renting Nvidia compute through data centers in countries such as Thailand and Singapore, The Information reported in August, though export-control lawyers told the outlet the agency lacks clear authority to regulate remote access under current law.

In June, the value of Zhipu, a Chinese AI firm, reached around $170 billion on the Hong Kong stock market, higher than those of Xiaomi and BYD. It had listed just five months earlier, with a market capitalization of around $7 billion. Zhipu's main business is developing frontier AI models. With no way to invest in OpenAI or Anthropic, people invested in Zhipu instead.

Then, on July 16th, another Chinese AI firm, Moonshot, unveiled a new model, Kimi K3. With 2.8 trillion parameters, it was touted as the biggest open model in the world. Within hours of its release, it had risen to first place on a popular leaderboard for coding models.

The next day, Zhipu's share price plunged 28%, wiping out about $26 billion in value in a single day. Nothing had gone wrong at Zhipu. But Moonshot's founder was a former student of Zhipu's founder, the Tsinghua professor Tang Jie, and over the past week, Chinese media had framed the competition between the two firms as a battle between master and disciple. JPMorgan cut its price target for Zhipu's stock by a third, arguing that since frontier AI models now advance so quickly, the premium for being the leader would have to shrink.

As one Chinese business publication put it, the shelf life of a lead shrunk. That was what the market was paying for. It wasn't paying for Zhipu's models. It was paying for Zhipu to stay ahead.

In China, staying ahead lasted about a month. Zhipu had released a new model a month before K3, and Alibaba and DeepSeek and MiniMax released new models right behind K3.

Still, Zhipu's business kept growing. In the first half of this year, its revenue rose to around four times what it had been a year earlier, and more than all of last year.

The stock is now down more than 80% from its highs.

So when the Financial Times says the Chinese AI bubble has already burst, it wasn't Chinese AI that failed. It burst because Chinese labs are catching up to each other so fast that investors can't justify paying up for a winner.

American labs haven't faced this test yet because nobody could invest in them until now. But with Anthropic's prospectus just out, investors are about to learn whether leads last any longer in the US than they did in China.
